newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nikko, Smith Barney tie-up seen aiding Japan funds.
newsitem.headline: Nikko, Smith Barney tie-up seen aiding Japan funds.

text.p: A venture between Nikko Securities Co and Smith Barney should be a boon for Japan's investment trusts, which have long lagged their more popular and sophisticated U.S. and British counterparts, analysts said.
"This is an opportunity to change Japanese people's image of investment trusts," said Yoshinobu Yamada, an analyst at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc.

Nikko said on Friday that it would set up a joint consulting venture in Tokyo with Smith Barney International Inc to issue evaluations of Japanese investment trusts, the equivalent of mutual funds in the United States and unit trusts in Britain.

"Japan's investment trust funds have not become popular yet and if there is a company which assesses the performance of funds with an objective view, it will help boost their attractiveness," a Nikko official said.
The joint venture will initially offer software and systems that can be used to make customised asset allocation models for investment trusts, a Nikko official said.
In its early stages, he added, the venture will employ 10 to 20 analysts to assess the performance of funds offered by Japanese investment trust managers.
Further details on the equally owned venture will be decided by late October, he said.

Without an established system to measure the performance of Japanese trusts, the popular perception is that they are so poorly run that ordinary, individual investors are not interested in them despite their popularity abroad.

Traditionally, most such trusts have been managed by securities houses' trust management subsidiaries, which are expected to unload unattractive stocks left over from an unsuccessful underwriting or collecting dust in inventories.

In addition, salesmen may try to persuade small investors to trade investment trusts unnecessarily often, resulting in higher brokering commissions for the salesmen but poorer performance for the trusts.

The Nikko official said the brokerage eventually intends to offer so-called "consultant wrap accounts", which involve discretionary management contracts or the introduction of fund managers to investors.
It may be some time, however, before the venture is able to introduce eligible fund managers to customers, as the collection of data about individual managers will be a time-consuming task, he said.

Tie-ups between Japanese and foreign financial firms that target specific areas are expected to increase as a result of Japan's "Big Bang" reforms, which are intended to allocate the country's 1,200 trillion yen in individual financial assets more effectively.
Foreign securities houses with experience in developing attractive investment products are keen to expand into investment trusts and asset management in Japan.

Fidelity Brokerage Services (Japan), a unit of Fidelity Brokerage Services Inc, recently received a licence to deal, broker and sell securities in Tokyo in order to make direct sales of Fidelity's mutual funds.
Merrill Lynch International Capital Management, a Japanese unit of Merrill Lynch Asset Management LP, intends to enter the investment trust sector later this year.
Japanese banks are also paying close attention to investment trusts, which they will be allowed to sell over-the-counter within a year or so.
